title: Was There Evidence That Poor Teaching Was a Significant Problem at South San?
subtitles: Were Teachers Really What South San Needed to Fix? — Part 2
excerpt: Before South San’s Board of Managers approved districtwide NIET/TAP on April 14, 2025, what evidence showed that deficiencies in teaching practice were a major cause of low student performance? This article follows the timeline of what the district had identified, what was presented before the vote, what was still being studied, and what remains unclear about the evidence behind the decision.

sections.content: If you haven’t read Part 1, start here.

In an effort to improve student performance, South San adopted NIET/TAP, a model that puts changing teacher practice at the center of its improvement strategy. Teachers are trained, coached, observed, and evaluated against prescribed instructional practices. But before asking whether NIET/TAP was the right solution, there is a more basic question:
Was ineffective teaching actually a significant problem at South San?

To answer that, we started before Superintendent Hinojosa arrived and before TEA appointed the new Board of Managers. We looked at what South San itself had already identified as its major needs and challenges, then followed the public record forward to see what changed, what evidence was presented, and when.
South San NIET/TAP Timeline
https://southsaneducationexplained.org/preview.html?src=assets%2Fuploads%2Fimages%2FPDF%20slide%20ss%20timeline%20part%202.png&name=PDF%20slide%20ss%20timeline%20part%202.png
sections.caption: South San’s identified needs before April 14, 2025, and the evidence publicly presented when districtwide NIET/TAP was approved. PDF attachment description:

sections.content: What the Timeline Shows So Far

We started by looking for South San’s March 2024 Comprehensive Needs Assessment, but the district’s original PDF is no longer available at its former web address. Search engines still retain indexed text captured when the PDF was publicly available, even though the document itself is no longer online.
That indexed text shows that the assessment’s formal staff-quality concern was teacher turnover, not ineffective teaching. Other identified problems included learning loss, curriculum and intervention systems, data use, and related district processes.

Then came April 14, 2025. TEA Conservator Abe Saavedra told the Board that “over the next several weeks” he would conduct a new Needs Assessment with Hinojosa and district staff. He said the completed assessment would be presented to the Board and used to identify specific goals for the district. At that same meeting—before that assessment had been completed—Hinojosa recommended districtwide NIET/TAP, and the Board of Managers approved it 7–0.

That raised another question: Had the Board already considered districtwide NIET/TAP somewhere else? We reviewed the Board’s public meeting calendar and posted meeting records leading up to April 14. We found no public record showing earlier Board consideration of districtwide NIET/TAP.
South San had worked with NIET before, previously in a limited capacity, but that was much different from what was being proposed in April 2025.

So we looked at the April 14 vote itself. Hinojosa described NIET/TAP and asked whether Board members had any questions. No Board member asked a question about the proposal. After a motion and second, the chair again invited discussion or questions. None followed, and the Board approved districtwide NIET/TAP 7–0.
What South San-specific evidence had Board members reviewed before voting?

At this point, the public record gave us the sequence—but not the answer. The new Needs Assessment was still pending, we had found no earlier public Board consideration of districtwide NIET/TAP, and no Board member asked a question when it came up for approval. What we still had not found was the South San-specific evidence showing that problems with teaching were a major cause of low student performance.
So We Looked at What the Board Was Given

The official Board record includes an eight-page attachment for the April 14 NIET/TAP agenda item. It includes the agenda summary and NIET’s Statement of Work for districtwide TAP support at 12 schools, totaling $252,500. In the attachment, we found no South San-specific data showing how widespread problems with teaching were, no analysis connecting those problems to low student performance, and no root-cause analysis identifying teaching practice as a major cause of the district’s academic results.
So What Did the Board of Managers Review Before Voting?
The public record does not tell us what additional South San-specific evidence, if any, individual Board members reviewed before voting. So we asked them directly.
We Asked the Board of Managers

On September 8, 2026, we sent questions individually to each member of the Board of Managers asking what role they personally played in reviewing the evidence before the April 14 vote, what South San-specific evidence they reviewed before approving districtwide NIET/TAP, whether the promised Needs Assessment or root-cause analysis was completed, and where the public can review that evidence. As of September 25, 2026, no responses had been received. If a response is received, it will be posted here.
View Board responses and updates.
But the story did not end with the April 14 vote.

Four months later, the Board met for an August 25 workshop. This time, Hinojosa and his team presented what was described as their “data analysis and root cause.” During the discussion, Hinojosa asked for a “PowerPoint presentation,” and Board members referred to slides—including one about “building teacher capacity.”
Was this the analysis that finally showed why teaching practice had become such a major focus—and what did it actually show?
Click here to see what we found next.

title: Why Did South San Change How Teachers Teach?
subtitles: Were Teachers Really What South San Needed to Fix? - Part 1
excerpt: TEA replaced South San’s elected Board primarily to address longstanding governance and management problems. Yet less than two months later, the new Board moved to substantially restructure classroom instruction districtwide by approving NIET/TAP, a management-style model that shifts instructional decision-making toward district-directed expectations and monitoring. What is NIET/TAP—and was deficient teaching really a significant enough problem at South San to warrant such a rapid districtwide restructuring of classroom instruction?

sections.content: A Bit of Background: Why Did TEA Replace South San’s Board?

On February 19, 2025, TEA replaced South San’s elected Board of Trustees with a seven-member Board of Managers after years of documented governance problems, financial-control concerns, and repeated state investigations. Unlike TEA interventions triggered by academic accountability failures, South San’s intervention was rooted primarily in longstanding problems with district governance and management.
TEA Intervened Over Board Mismanagement—but South San Quickly Moved to Restructure Classroom Instruction

Yet less than two months later, on April 14, 2025, the newly installed Board of Managers, acting on the superintendent’s recommendation, approved districtwide implementation of NIET/TAP, an outside-developed school-improvement model—before a new district Needs Assessment announced at that same meeting had been completed.

That decision affected both how teachers were expected to teach and how their teaching would be monitored and evaluated. Under NIET/TAP, teachers were expected to follow prescribed instructional practices, with coaching, observation, and evaluation tied to how those expectations were implemented. At the same time, South San’s broader curriculum requirements affected the materials teachers could use and how much latitude they had to adapt instruction to differences among students.
What is NIET/TAP?

The model South San adopted was developed outside of the district. TAP (The System for Teacher and Student Advancement) was introduced in 1999 by Lowell Milken, whose professional background was in law, business, and philanthropy rather than classroom teaching. He later founded the National Institute for Excellence in Teaching (NIET).

At its core, NIET/TAP reflects a management-oriented theory of school improvement: define expected instructional practices, train and coach teachers toward them, observe and evaluate how those practices are implemented, and use performance measures to track results. The model is built on the idea that more consistent implementation of those expected practices will lead to improved student performance.
How is NIET/TAP changing teaching in South San classrooms?

In practice, NIET/TAP places a detailed, externally developed framework around decisions teachers would otherwise make more independently. Teachers—who bring subject expertise, professional training, experience, and day-to-day knowledge of their students—are expected to work within those prescribed practices and expectations, leaving less room to innovate, draw on their individual strengths, develop their own solutions to classroom problems, and find new ways to engage and inspire students.
What Does This Mean for Students?

Much of the real work of education happens in the moments when teachers use their knowledge, experience, creativity, and relationships with students to respond to what a class or an individual student needs. When teachers have less freedom to make those judgments, students may also lose some of the flexibility, creativity, individual attention, and responsiveness that can help them learn, stay engaged, and succeed.
What Evidence Justified This Level of Intervention in Classroom Teaching?
Was teacher effectiveness really a major cause of low student performance—and what evidence did South San have for that conclusion?
Let’s see what the public evidence actually shows.
